subtitle: Learn what organizational culture is, read it at three levels in DSD meetings, notices and supervision, and use the idea of cultural tensions to talk about workplace norms without blaming people.
audience: For all DHS and DSD staff, supervisors and leaders. This is the first module in the Culture, Power, and Organizational Norms path and assumes no prior background.

lessons.title: What organizational culture is, and why it holds
objectives: Explain organizational culture as shared, learned assumptions about how work gets done.
Describe why culture persists after the people and problems that shaped it have changed.
Distinguish examining a culture from judging the character of the people in it.
Identify one way culture is taught to new members of a team.
lessons.teaching:
Every work group develops ways of doing things that stop feeling like choices. A team learns how early people arrive for a meeting, whether it is safe to say 'I don't know,' how polished a draft must be before a supervisor sees it, and which deadlines are firm and which can bend. Very little of this is written down. People learn it by watching others, by being corrected, and by noticing what gets praised and what gets ignored. That shared and mostly unspoken learning is what this path means by organizational culture.

Edgar Schein, an organizational psychologist at the MIT Sloan School of Management, offered a definition that much later writing builds on. In a 1983 working paper, Schein described culture as the pattern of basic assumptions that a group has invented, discovered or developed as it learned to deal with its problems, and that is taught to new members as the correct way to perceive, think and feel about those problems. Three parts of that definition matter for public service. Culture is learned, so it can be examined and relearned. It belongs to a group rather than to any one person. And it began as a solution to a real problem, which is why it usually feels reasonable to the people inside it.

That last point explains why culture holds. Consider how this works in practice. A habit that once solved a problem, such as an extra review step added after a costly error or a meeting format that kept a crisis organized, keeps going after the problem has changed. Schein observed that a value which works over time can become an assumption that is taken for granted and is no longer open to debate. Staff turn over, programs change and the people served change, yet the habit stays because it has become simply how things are done here. A large organization also holds more than one culture. DHS as an agency, DSD as a division, individual units, and professions such as case management, policy and data analysis each carry their own assumptions, and those assumptions can differ or pull against one another.

Examining a culture is not the same as judging the people in it. When a team asks why drafts always pass through four reviews, the question is what the practice assumes and what it produces, not whether the people who follow it are careful or careless. This path keeps that distinction throughout. It does not score anyone, rank teams or treat finishing a module as evidence that anything has changed. Culture shows itself in the work, so any change also has to show up in the work: in clearer notices, fairer decisions and barriers that are actually removed.
lessons.keyPoint: Organizational culture is the set of shared, learned assumptions about how work gets done. It began as a solution to real problems, which is why it feels reasonable from the inside and why it lasts after conditions change.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} joined a DSD unit three weeks ago. In a one-on-one check-in, {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} tells {{SUPERVISOR}} that no one explained the unwritten rules. Drafts seem to need a senior reviewer's approval before anyone else sees them, and people rarely ask questions in the team meeting but ask many afterward in chat. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} asks whether these are policies or just habits. {{SUPERVISOR}} realizes that some of them are habits nobody has examined in years.
lessons.question: What is the most useful response from {{SUPERVISOR}}?
choices: Reassure {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} that everyone adjusts in time and the habits will soon feel natural.
Thank {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} for noticing, sort which practices come from a written requirement and which are habits, and ask what the habits seem to accomplish.
Tell the team that the newest member has found problems with how the unit works and ask people to explain themselves.
feedback: Adjusting is real, but this response teaches the habits as the correct way without asking whether they still serve their purpose. A newer colleague's view is one of the few chances to see the culture from outside.
This treats the observation as useful information, separates required steps from learned habits, and keeps the focus on what the practices do rather than on who follows them.
Presenting the observation as a complaint puts {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} in an awkward position and invites defensiveness. The practices can be examined without asking anyone to answer for them.
lessons.reflection: Think back to your first weeks in your current unit, or use the practice case. Privately note one thing you learned by watching rather than by being told. Does it still make sense to you, and do you know where it came from?
lessons.action: List three things a new person on your team would need to learn that are not written down anywhere. For each one, note whether you know where it came from and what problem it was meant to solve.

check.question: According to Schein's definition, where does organizational culture come from?
check.correct: Assumptions a group developed while dealing with its problems, which are then taught to new members as the correct way to see and act.
wrong: The personality of the organization's most senior leader.
The mission statement and values the organization has written down and posted.
check.feedback: Schein describes culture as learned group assumptions that began as solutions to problems. Leaders shape culture and stated values are part of it, but neither one is the whole of it.

lessons.title: Three levels: what you see, what is said, what is assumed
objectives: Describe Schein's three levels of culture: artifacts, espoused values and basic underlying assumptions.
Explain why artifacts are easy to see but hard to interpret.
Recognize a gap between stated values and everyday practice without assuming bad faith.
Write a tentative assumption that could explain a practice you observe.
lessons.teaching:
Schein described culture at three levels, ordered from the most visible to the least. Artifacts are what you can see, hear and handle: the layout of a workspace, how people show up on a video call, the format of an agenda, the templates a unit relies on, the documents it produces, and the stories people tell about past successes and mistakes. Espoused values are the reasons a group gives for what it does, such as statements about person-centered practice, respect or transparency. Basic underlying assumptions are the beliefs people no longer notice they hold, about what counts as good work, who is the expert, how fast is fast enough and what is safe to say out loud.

Schein cautioned that artifacts are tricky. They are easy to observe and hard to decipher, because we can see what a group does without seeing the reasoning behind it. Two units might both keep cameras off in meetings, one because people work from shared spaces where others could be seen, the other because people feel watched. The artifact is identical; the meaning is not. So the honest way to read an artifact is to treat any explanation as a guess to check with the people involved rather than as a conclusion. An outsider, including a newer colleague, can see artifacts clearly and still misread what they mean.

Espoused values matter, and they are not the same thing as practice. Schein noted that the reasons people give for a behavior may not be the reasons that actually drive it. A division might say it values the input of people who use its services, and also hold every advisory meeting at a time and in a format that only some of those people can manage. Naming that gap is not an accusation of hypocrisy. Stated values often describe what a group is trying to become. The gap is useful because it points to an assumption that is currently stronger than the stated value, such as an assumption that serious work happens during business hours or that a written comment carries more weight than a spoken one.

The deepest level shapes behavior the most and is the hardest to examine. Peter Senge, writing about learning organizations, made a related point: what people carry in their heads are assumptions, and these mental pictures of how the world works strongly influence how they perceive problems and opportunities. You cannot observe an assumption directly. You infer it from patterns in the artifacts and from the distance between what is said and what is done, and then you test the inference with others. A good working habit is to phrase it tentatively, for example: it looks as if we assume a decision is not real until there is a written memo, and I wonder whether that is true. Phrasing it that way invites a group to examine the assumption together instead of defending it.
lessons.keyPoint: Read culture at three levels: the artifacts you can see, the values people state, and the assumptions people no longer notice. Treat any interpretation as a guess to test with the people involved.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is reviewing how a DSD policy team gathers input on draft guidance. The team's values statement says it centers the voices of people who use services. In practice, comments come through a written online form open for ten business days, and the summary includes only comments that cite a specific section of the draft. {{CASE_MANAGER}}, who works closely with families, mentions that several families shared detailed concerns by phone, and those concerns were never counted.
lessons.question: How should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} describe what is happening?
choices: As a likely gap between a stated value and an underlying assumption about what counts as a usable comment, to check with the team and with the families involved.
As proof that the team does not really care about the people who use services.
As a minor process detail that does not need to be connected to the team's values.
feedback: This names the gap without assigning motives, offers a tentative assumption that can be tested, and keeps the people who were left out part of the conversation.
The gap is real information, but it does not show what anyone cares about. Treating it as a verdict on character makes the assumption harder to examine, not easier.
Process details are where assumptions live. Separating them from the team's stated values leaves the gap in place and the phone comments uncounted.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider one value your unit or division states often. Where does everyday practice match it well, and where might an unspoken assumption be stronger than the stated value? You may use the practice case instead of your own setting.
lessons.action: Pick one recurring artifact in your work, such as a meeting agenda, a template or a standard email. Write down one stated value it is meant to serve and one assumption it might carry, phrased as a question you could ask your team.

check.question: Why did Schein describe artifacts as the tricky level of culture?
check.correct: They are easy to observe but hard to interpret without understanding the assumptions behind them.
wrong: They are hidden and can be found only through formal surveys.
They always match the organization's stated values exactly.
check.feedback: Artifacts are the visible layer, so anyone can see them. Their meaning depends on assumptions that are not visible, which is why interpretations need to be checked with the people involved.

lessons.title: Where culture shows up in DSD work: meetings, notices and supervision
objectives: Identify cultural assumptions in three everyday settings: meetings, written notices and supervision.
Explain how a notice can carry assumptions about its reader.
Describe how supervision teaches culture through what is asked about, praised and corrected.
Choose one routine to observe with fresh eyes and one small change to try.
lessons.teaching:
Culture is easiest to study in routines that happen so often that no one questions them. In DSD, as in most public agencies, three of those routines are meetings, written communication with the public, and supervision. Each is a place where a group's assumptions are practiced and handed on, and each is a place where a small change can be tried and its effects observed. Looking at these routines closely does not require special tools, only the willingness to describe what actually happens before deciding what it means.

Meetings show who is expected to speak, whose knowledge counts and how decisions are actually made. Look at who sets the agenda, how much time goes to updates compared with discussion, whether questions are welcomed during the meeting or saved for side conversations afterward, and whether a decision is recorded or simply assumed. Notice whether people who join by phone, work with an interpreter or need materials ahead of time receive what they need early enough to take part. None of these features is good or bad on its own. Each reflects an assumption about how a group should work, and each affects who is able to contribute.

Notices and other written materials carry assumptions about their readers. A notice written in dense language and organized around the agency's process rather than the reader's next step assumes a reader with time, reading confidence and familiarity with the system. The federal plain language guidelines ask public writers to put the reader first, use common words and short sentences, and say clearly what the reader must do. A notice can be legally accurate and still be hard to use. When a team defends a format mainly because it has always been written that way, the format has become an artifact of the culture, and the assumptions it carries are worth examining. Formal notice requirements still apply, so any change goes through the people responsible for them.

Supervision teaches culture more directly than almost anything else, often without anyone intending it. What a supervisor asks about in a check-in signals what matters, whether that is caseload numbers, quality of contact, workload or learning. How mistakes are received teaches whether it is safe to raise problems early. Amy Edmondson's field study of work teams found that team psychological safety, a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, was associated with learning behavior such as asking questions and discussing errors. The finding is an association rather than a guarantee, but it gives supervisors good reason to notice how their responses land. A supervisor who meets a reported error by asking what got in the way, rather than who is at fault, is teaching an assumption. So is a supervisor who meets it with visible frustration. Both are culture in practice.
lessons.keyPoint: Meetings, notices and supervision are where a group practices and teaches its assumptions every day. Observable details, such as who speaks, who a notice is written for and how mistakes are received, reveal the culture.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}} notices that in weekly team meetings the same three experienced staff do most of the talking, while {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} and two others send their questions privately afterward. Later, in a one-on-one, {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} mentions finding an error in a letter template that has been in use for months, but hesitated to raise it because it might look like criticism of the people who wrote it.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} do first?
choices: Require every team member to speak at least once in each meeting.
Correct the template quietly and leave the meeting format as it is.

Thank {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} for raising the error, fix it through the usual process, and try a meeting change, such as a standing time for questions and template issues, then ask the team whether it helped.
feedback: Required speaking can add pressure without addressing why people hold back. It treats the symptom rather than the assumption about who should speak.
Fixing the error matters, but the hesitation is also information. Leaving the meeting format unchanged teaches that problems are safer raised privately, if they are raised at all.
This receives the report in a way that makes raising problems safer, handles the fix properly, and tests a small change with the team instead of assuming it will work.
lessons.reflection: Think about a meeting you attend regularly, or use the practice case. Privately note who usually speaks, who usually does not, and what the quieter people might add if the format were different. Describe the pattern without naming or diagnosing anyone.
lessons.action: For one week, observe one routine: a recurring meeting, a notice your unit sends, or your own supervisory check-ins. Write down three observable features and the assumption each might reflect. Choose one small change to try and decide how you will learn whether it helped.

check.question: What did Edmondson's study of work teams find about psychological safety?
check.correct: It was associated with learning behaviors such as asking questions and discussing errors.
wrong: It guarantees that teams will make fewer mistakes.
It means team members never disagree or feel uncomfortable.
check.feedback: The study found an association between psychological safety and learning behavior. It does not promise results, and psychological safety concerns being able to take interpersonal risks, which often includes disagreeing.

lessons.title: Cultural tensions in public service
objectives: Describe six cultural tensions common in public service work.
Explain why both sides of each tension serve a legitimate purpose.
Recognize the pattern that develops when one side of a tension always wins.
Locate where Modules 2 and 3 of the path continue this work.
lessons.teaching:
Part of what makes culture hard to talk about is that the habits in question usually serve something real. Speed matters when people are waiting for services. Expertise matters when a decision affects someone's health or safety. Standard procedures protect fairness and make work possible to review. Conversations about culture tend to stall when they are framed as good habits against bad ones, because everyone can point to what their habit protects. The One DSD framework uses a different frame: cultural tensions, which are pairs of values that both belong in public service and that need to be held in balance.

The framework names six tensions. Efficiency and participation: getting decisions made, and including the people those decisions affect. Expertise and lived experience: professional knowledge, and the knowledge of people who live with a program's effects. Standardization and accessibility: consistent processes, and processes that work for people with different needs. Productivity and well-being: the amount of work produced, and the health of the people producing it. Control and shared leadership: clear accountability, and decisions made together with others. Speed and thoughtfulness: acting quickly, and taking time to check assumptions. Neither side of any pair is the problem.

The pattern to watch for is what happens when one side always dominates. If efficiency always wins, participation shrinks to a formality and the same voices shape every decision. If standardization always wins, the people whose needs fall outside the standard carry the cost, often quietly. If productivity always wins, exhaustion starts to look normal and mistakes become harder to admit. Because each habit protects something real, the imbalance is difficult to see from the inside. That is what makes the tension frame useful. It lets a team say, without accusing anyone, that the balance in a particular routine has tipped. It also opens four questions that keep the discussion on the work: who benefits from the current balance, who is burdened by it, whose voice shapes it, and who is left out of it.

The rest of this path builds on these ideas. Module 2 looks at how cultural assumptions harden into systems, the rules, forms, timelines and resources that carry norms forward after the people who set them have moved on. Module 3 introduces Tema Okun's writing on white supremacy culture as one reflective lens among several. Okun names characteristics, such as perfectionism and a sense of urgency, that can become normal in organizations, and cautions against using the framework to accuse people. That module presents both the framework's strengths and the critiques of it. For now, it is enough to notice that some of the tensions above, such as speed against thoughtfulness, are also named in that writing, and that the aim of examining any of them is better work, not blame.
lessons.keyPoint: Both sides of each cultural tension serve public service. Trouble starts when one side always wins, so ask which way a routine has tipped and who carries the cost.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD workgroup is redesigning an intake step. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} has a firm date from leadership and proposes finalizing the design with the internal team and sharing it afterward. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, a county partner, asks to test a draft with a few people who have recently been through intake. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} worries that testing will cause the team to miss the date. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}} worries that the design will repeat a barrier the county sees often.
lessons.question: How could the workgroup use the tension frame?
choices: Decide which person is right, since the deadline and the testing request cannot both be honored.
Name the tension between speed and thoughtfulness, ask what the date actually requires, and look for a limited test that fits the timeline, recording what could not be tested.
Delay the project until full community engagement is complete, regardless of leadership's timeline.
feedback: Either-or framing turns a tension into a contest. Both concerns protect something real, and the workgroup loses information by picking a winner.
This keeps both values in view, checks the real constraint, and looks for a way to honor both. Recording what could not be tested keeps the tradeoff visible for later review.
Thoughtfulness matters, but ignoring a real timeline tips the balance the other way and may go beyond the workgroup's authority. The aim is balance, not reversal.
lessons.reflection: Look over the six tensions privately. In your own work, which one seems most often to tip toward one side? Who benefits from that balance, and who might be carrying the cost?
lessons.action: Choose one recurring decision in your work, such as how a meeting agenda is set or how a form is revised. Identify which cultural tension it involves, which side usually wins, and one small way to give the other side more room. Bring the observation to a colleague or your team as a question.

check.question: What is the main risk the cultural tensions frame asks teams to watch for?
check.correct: One side of a legitimate pair of values winning so consistently that the other side, and the people it protects, lose out.
wrong: Any use of deadlines, expertise or standard procedures in public service.
Disagreement between colleagues about how work should be done.
check.feedback: Both sides of each tension are legitimate, so the frame does not reject deadlines, expertise or standards. It flags a pattern of consistent imbalance, and disagreement is often how a team first notices that pattern.

cards.back: The shared, learned assumptions a group developed while dealing with its problems, taught to new members as the correct way to see and act (Schein).
The visible level of culture: layouts, agendas, templates, documents and the stories people tell. Easy to see and hard to interpret.
The reasons a group gives for what it does. They matter, and they may differ from what actually drives behavior.
Beliefs people no longer notice they hold. The deepest level of culture, inferred from patterns and tested with others rather than observed directly.
Senge's term for the assumptions people carry about how the world works, which shape how they perceive problems and opportunities.
A shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as asking questions or raising errors. Associated with team learning in Edmondson's research.
A pair of legitimate values, such as speed and thoughtfulness, that need to be held in balance. The risk is one side always winning.

aid.heading: Read the three levels
items: Write down what you can see or hear: the artifact.
Write down what people say it is for: the espoused value.
Write a tentative assumption that might explain it, phrased as a question.
Check your interpretation with the people involved before treating it as true.

aid.heading: Look at everyday routines
items: Meetings: who sets the agenda, who speaks, how decisions are recorded, and who can take part fully.
Notices: who the reader is assumed to be, and whether the notice says plainly what to do next. Formal notice requirements still apply.
Supervision: what you ask about, what you praise, and how you respond when someone reports a mistake.

aid.heading: Use the tension frame
items: Name the pair of values involved, such as efficiency and participation.
Ask which way the routine usually tips.
Ask who benefits, who is burdened, whose voice shapes it and who is left out.

aid.heading: Keep it about the work
items: Describe practices and their effects, not people's character or motives.
Do not score or rank individuals or teams.
Formal employment, accommodation and civil-rights decisions stay with Human Resources and the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division.
Look for change in the work itself, such as a clearer notice or a barrier removed.

sources.title: Edgar H. Schein, Organizational Culture: A Dynamic Model, MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper 1412-83 (February 1983), DSpace@MIT
sources.note: Supports the definition of culture as a group's learned basic assumptions taught to new members, the three levels of artifacts, espoused values and basic assumptions, the caution that artifacts are easy to see but hard to decipher, and the observation that a value that works can become an unexamined assumption (lessons 1 and 2). An early statement of Schein's model, which Schein's later books develop further.

sources.title: Peter M. Senge, The Leader's New Work: Building Learning Organizations, Sloan Management Review 32, no. 1 (Fall 1990)
sources.note: Supports the description of mental models as largely unspoken assumptions that shape how people perceive problems and opportunities (lesson 2). Read in the publisher's PDF view. A conceptual article drawn from Senge's book The Fifth Discipline, not an empirical study.

sources.title: Edmondson, A. — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams, Administrative Science Quarterly (1999)
sources.note: Supports the definition of team psychological safety and its association with learning behavior in a field study of work teams (lesson 3). Findings are associational. The supervision examples are the program's own.

sources.title: PlainLanguage.gov, Federal plain language guidelines
sources.note: Supports the guidance that public writing should put the reader first, use common words and short sentences, and say clearly what the reader must do (lesson 3). Federal guidance; formal notice requirements for DHS programs still apply.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: Cited only for the brief pointer in lesson 4 to characteristics such as perfectionism and a sense of urgency, and to the author's caution against using the framework to accuse people. Module 3 treats the framework, its strengths and its critiques in depth.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency policy on considering equity in daily work and using the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions across policy, budgets, procurement, hiring and service delivery. This course is learning material, not a substitute for the policy.
